items.title: Overview
items.text:
Participants will be tested on the content below:

I. For each object in the lists below, identify and explain: * surface/atmospheric features * processes (e.g., cryovolcanism) * properties of specific objects:

1. Objects in the Solar System: 
    1a. Venus 
    1b. Mars 
    1c. Ganymede 
    1d. Europa 
    1e. Enceladus 
    1f. Titan 
    1g. Makemake 
    1h. 101955 Bennu 
    1i. 67P/Churyumov—Gerasimenko

2. Extrasolar Systems: 
    2a. TRAPPIST-1 
    2b. Kepler-452 
    3c. LHS 1140

II. Habitability beyond the Earth: 

3. Conditions relevant to habitability, including:
    3a. temperature 
    3b. atmospheric composition and retention 
    3c. presence of stable liquids (surface and subsurface) 
    3c. tidal heating 
    3d. chemical disequilibrium

4. Geologic and chemical evidence of habitability, including:
    4a. historical evidence of liquid water from morphology 
    4b. surface/atmospheric composition inferred spectral features 
    4c. delivery of water and organic material from small 
        Solar System bodies


5.  Biology and chemistry relevant to habitability, including:
    5a. building blocks of life 
        * proteins nucleic acids, lipids, carbohydrates), 
    5b. phases/forms of water 
        *liquid
        * amorphous and crystalline ice brines
        * clathrates
    5c. extremophiles 
        * chemolithoautotrophs
        * tardigrades

III. General engineering principles and facilities including: * science objectives * instrumentation * tradeoffs underlying spacecraft and telescope design

6. Exoplanet detection techniques, limited to 
    6a. transits
    6b. radial velocity
    6c. microlensing, 
    6d. direct imaging.

7. Space Missions to solar system objects
    7a. DAVINCI 
    7b. VERITAS 
    7c. Perseverance 
    7d. Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter 
    7e. MAVEN 
    7f. ESCAPADE 
    7g. Galileo
    7h. Europa Clipper 
    7i. JUICE 
    7j. Cassini-Huygens 
    7k. Dragonfly 
    7l. OSIRIS-REx 
    7m. Rosetta

8. Space Telescopes for observng extra-solar-system objects:
    8a. Kepler Space Telescope 
    8b. James Webb Space Telescope
    8c. Roman Space Telescope 
    8d. Habitable Worlds Observatory

IV. Mathematical concepts emphasizing algebraic manipulation. * rearranging/deriving equations * order of magnitude estimation * dimensional analysis * sketching graphs * proportions 

9. Light radiation, and temperature 
    9a. Doppler shift 
    9b. flux 
    9c. inverse-square law 
    9d. albedo 
    9e. the Stefan—Boltzmann law 
    9f. Wien’s displacement law 
    9g. equilibrium temperature _

10. Gravity orbits, and tides: 
    10a. kinetic and potential energy 
    10b. Newton’s law of gravitation 
    10c. Kepler’s laws 
    10d. escape velocity 
    10e. tidal forces

11. Chemistry: 
    11a. ideal gas law 
    11b. kinetics (e.g. Arrhenius equation)
    11c chemical equilibrium

items.title: Why focus on low-mass stars?
items.text:
Compared to massive stars:

  • Low-mass stars are more common. So the neighborhood of the Sun is more likely to be crowded with low-mass stars than high-mass stars.

  • Low-mass stars are smaller. So when a planet-sized objects eclipses a low-mass star, it hides a larger fraction of its surface.

  • Low-mass stars have lower mass, so planet-sized objects will cause a relatively larger perturbation in the star's radial velocity.

See further details on the Trappis-1 planetary system, the LHS 1140 system, and the Kepler 452 system.

See also this comprehensive report from the National Science Foundation on "The State of the Field of Exoplanets".

items.title: Objects beyond the Solar System
items.text:
The following stars are of interest for studying our own solar system because recent observations have shown evidence that they have a planetary system.

  • For some of these stars, a disk of gas and dust has been detected around them; presumably, planets will form out of these disks.

  • For other stars, a large planet has been detected, and much if not all of the original debris disk has by now dissipated.

Name Type Evidence of a Planetary System HL Tauri A very young star in Taurus a debris disk Beta Pictoris A young star a debris disk and an exoplanet HD 209458 An main-sequence star a known exoplanet 51 Pegasi An evolved star a known (large) exoplanet

items.title: Kepler 452
items.text:
The planets associated with Kepler-452 was discovered by the Kepler Space Telescope, launched on March 7, 2009. The telescope had a diameter of 2.7m, and, being space-borne, suffered none of the atmospheric effects that blur astronomical images.

Kepler searched a single patch of sky (115 square degrees, roughly 12-16 degrees in diameter) in the constellations Cygnus and Lyra, and monitored approximately 150,000 stars in that region.

The Kepler telescope repeatedly measured the position of each star they detected; those with the highest proper motions were the nearest, and therefore best candidates for finding planetary companions.

Kepler watched for small dips in star brightness when a planet crossed in front of a star.

By this means, it discovered 2,784 exoplanets; 2,000 additional planetary candidates await confirmation.

The Kepler Space Telescope ran out of fuel on October 30, 2018.

Kepler-452b is called Earth's "older cousin" because it is the first near-Earth-size planet found orbiting in the habitable zone of a G-type, sun-like star rather than a dim red dwarf. This match in both star type and orbital conditions makes it a key milestone in the search for an Earth twin.

This 2024 NASA publication provides more detail.

items.title: LHS 1140-b
items.text:
LHS 1140-b was discovered by the MEarth project which is similar to the TRAPPIST project in that it uses robotically-run telescopes which are located in both hemispheres:

  • the Northern Hemisphere site is at Mt. Hopkins, AZ (just west of Tucson), and
  • the Southern Hemisphere site is at Cerro Tololo.

Unlike the TRAPPIST project, each site contains 8 telescopes, though each of the telescopes is smaller (16", 0.4m diamter) than the telescopes used in the TRAPPIST project.

items.title: Selecting target stars by proper motion
items.text: The LHS (Luyten Half-Second) Catalogue is a compilation of about 4000 stars that are moving fast relative to our solar system, and are therefore thought to be nearby. It was originally (1979) compiled from the photographic plates of the Palomar Observatory Sky Survey, combined with second-epoch plates (taken about 5 years after the first) of selected areas. A second Palomar Sky Survey was carried out in the 1990's, and its plates were contemporaneously digitized. The digitized version of the Second Survey, distributed in 2006, was the basis for the Revised LHS catalog.

items.title: Trappist 1
items.text:
TRAPPIST-1 is the name given to the first (and only) star with evidence of exoplanets found by the TRAPPIST facilities, a pair of matching 0.6m telescopes located

  • one in the Southern Hemisphere at La Silla in Chile;

  • one in the Northern Hemisphere at the Oukaimeden Observatory in Morocco.

The TRAPPIST telescopes and their operation are a Belgian project, named after the monks who brewed Belgian beers. The name is also an acronym for TRansiting Planets and Planetisimals and plAnetiesimals Small Portable Service Telescope.

Both TRAPPIST telescopes are robotic, i.e., run under computer control by a remote observer(s), possibly in Europe.

The TRAPPIST project focusses on ultra-cool dwarf stars drawn from public star catalogues, e.g., 2MASS.

The pilot catalog consisted of about 50-60 of the brightest southern ultra-cool dwarfs; only the star designated TRAPPIST-1 was found to have exoplanets.

The image below shows the field of view (1.6 arcmin \(\times\)\ 1.6 arcmin) as seen in visible light near TRAPPIST-1:

The innermost planets (b,c,d) lack thick atmospheres.

The following 4 planets are theoretically in the habitable zone.

  • TRAPPIST-1e: Widely considered the best candidate for life, with a size and energy input most similar to a rocky Earth-like world.

  • TRAPPIST-1f: Located a bit further out in a cooler region, potentially requiring thick greenhouse gases to maintain surface water.

  • TRAPPIST-1g: Sits near the outer edge of the zone, running the risk of being a cold, ice-covered world.

  • TRAPPIST-1d: Positioned on the inner edge; newer data suggests it might be too warm or lack a substantial atmosphere.

Note that, because these planets orbit close to the central star, they are all likely to be tidally locked, meaning the same side always faces the star.
